newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy mourns convicted murderer as fallen hero.
newsitem.headline: Italy mourns convicted murderer as fallen hero.

text.p: Italy on Thursday mourned the execution of Joseph O'Dell, a man who spoke no Italian, had no connection to Italy and yet became a rallying point for the country's fervent stand against the death penalty.

Flags were flying at half-mast in at least one Italian city on Thursday morning and Italians were observing a minute's silence for a man despised by many in the United States as a heartless rapist and killer.
O'Dell's execution on Wednesday night in Virginia despite appeals from Pope John Paul and Italian leaders, was treated in the media as if Italy had lost a native son or freedom fighter.
"Three O'Clock -- O'Dell Executed," ran the headline in Milan's Corriere della Sera newspaper, echoing the front-page, banner headline treatment the case has been receiving.
Turin's La Stampa called it "The New Frontier of the Barbarians" and La Repubblica of Rome ran a front page cartoon depicting O'Dell as a weary Christ carrying a cross to his execution on Calvary.
Italians held vigils in a number of cities during the night, following events in Virginia via live television hook-ups.
State television and a private broadcaster each ran three-and-a-half hour programmes from midnight until after O'Dell's execution by lethal injection.
Italy, which has no death penalty in civilian cases, is among the most vocal supporters of a worldwide ban.

The O'Dell case gradually became a cause celebre for opponents of capital punishment, with the Pope, President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro and Prime Minister Romano Prodi making appeals for clemency to Governor George Allen.
O'Dell was convicted for the 1985 rape and murder of Helen Schartner. U.S. officials denied O'Dell's request for new DNA testing he said would prove his innocence.
Most of the appeals, particularly the Pope's, did not enter into the guilty or innocent debate but were based on the position that only God could decide when to end a life.
There was no immediate comment from the Vatican, although O'Dell had asked in a letter that the Pope pray for him at the moment of his death as Christ had prayed for the good thief.

"We don't know everything about his (judicial) case .... but this does not rule out that a man and a Christian can oppose laws that decide life, which belongs only to God," Enzo Biagi, one of Italy's most respected commentators said.
But Biagi, writing in Corriere della Sera, said Mafia violence in southern mainland Italy and Sicily made the country anything but a shining example of respect for life.
Ironically, if one of O'Dell's last wishes is respected, he will be buried in the Sicilian capital, Palermo, where he has been made an honorary citizen.

"Palermo, which was for so many years a city of death and illegality has been striving for some time to become a symbol of life and legality," said Mayor Leoluca Orlando, who travelled to Virginia last week to appeal to Governor Allen for clemency.
"This is why we are fighting against the illegality of the death penalty...no-one, not even a state, can kill a human being," he said.
Orlando ordered flags flown at half-mast at the city hall and city employees observed a minute of silence before work.
Palermo officials said the city would pay for his body to be flown to Italy.
Luciano Neri, a parliamentarian of the Sicily-based La Rete party, said O'Dell, whom he visited recently, had asked that his grave in Palermo be made a monument against the death penalty.

The focal point of the overnight protests were in Rome's Campo de Fiori square, where hundreds of anti-death penalty activists gathered at the statue of Giordano Bruno, a monk burned there for heresy in 1600 during the Counter-Reformation.
They converged on the square after an earlier protest at the U.S. embassy, many of them wearing T-shirts reading: "Don't kill for me. I don't support the death penalty,"
